prose.kicker: The hardest-working defense in the league, assembled entirely out of other people's leftovers
prose.title: Real Deal Creel Bought a Superstar and Shoplifted the Rest
prose.dek: Keith Creelman spent {{f.team.0008.faa_spend}} at the Free Agent Auction and {{f.team.0008.idp_auction_share}} of his total on defense. Real Deal Creel finished {{f.team.0008.composite_rank}} of {{f.league.teams}}. Both of those facts are on purpose.

paragraphs: Puka Nacua is an Elite WR1 and he is the whole receiving corps. The room ranks {{f.team.0008.wr_rank}} in the league on his back, with Christian Watson at High-end WR3 next to him doing an impression of a starter. That is the shape of this whole roster in one line: one player nobody can match, and a supporting cast assembled at a discount.

Quarterback came out fine, if not the fireworks the price implied. Dak Prescott grades Mid QB1 and Kyler Murray Mid QB2 — a real superflex pair, no passengers, ranking {{f.team.0008.qb_rank}}. Keith paid {{f.team.0008.top_buy_price}} for Prescott, which is a lot of money for the eighth-best quarterback in a league where everyone needs two.

The backfield is the quiet success. Saquon Barkley at Mid RB1, Travis Etienne at Mid RB2, TreVeyon Henderson at High-end RB3, ranking {{f.team.0008.rb_rank}} — three genuine starters in a format where most teams are guessing at the flex by Halloween. Dallas Goedert grades Low-end TE1, which is not a hole, just the last chair in the room, and the position ranks {{f.team.0008.te_rank}}.

Then the defense, and this is where the article the numbers wanted to write is wrong. Three of seven defensive slots start players the production model calls replacement-level — Frankie Luvu, Chuck Clark, Gregory Rousseau — with Nick Bolton, Chamarri Conner, Josh Hines-Allen and Jalyx Hunt in the second tier behind them. Read that cold and you would say he forgot about defense.

He did not forget. Real Deal Creel has acquired {{f.team.0008.idp_adds_alltime}} defenders since the league started keeping the log, ranking {{f.team.0008.idp_adds_rank}} — the next team on that list has {{f.team.0008.idp_adds_next_best}}, and he has led the league in defensive pickups {{f.team.0008.idp_adds_lead_streak}} seasons running. Nobody else is close. He has also spent {{f.team.0008.idp_auction_spend}} on defenders at auction this year, {{f.team.0008.idp_auction_share}} of his money, out of the biggest budget in the league. That is not neglect, it is a policy: never pay retail for a linebacker, mine them off the wire instead, all season, forever.

The policy works, mostly. Points per started defender over the last three seasons puts him {{f.team.0008.idp_ppw_rank}} of {{f.league.teams}} — above the median, for almost nothing, which is a genuinely good trade. It is also not first, and the teams ahead of him did it by occasionally just buying a good defender. A Week One defense of three replacement-level starters is not a finished product; it is an opening inventory for a man who restocks it every week until December.

In April the roster held {{f.team.0008.active_roster_opening}} active players. The contracts still running were Goedert, Christian Watson, Henderson, Tetairoa McMillan, Marvin Harrison Jr, Trey Benson, Keon Coleman and Deshaun Watson, against {{f.team.0008.cap_opening}} of salary. That is a to-do list, not a team.

Draft night is where it got interesting. Real Deal Creel made three trades while the draft was live and used every pick he acquired within the hour. He sent the 1.04 to Gride, who took Jadarian Price with it, and got back Travis Etienne plus the 1.07 — which became KC Concepcion. He moved up in the second for De'Zhaun Stribling and up again in the third for Sonny Styles. Three trades, three picks, all spent the same night. Whatever else is true, the man does not sit on his hands.

By the time the Free Agent Auction opened the roster had reached {{f.team.0008.active_roster_preauction}} active players and the year had already turned once: McMillan out, Nacua in — Mid WR2 replaced by Elite WR1, the largest single upgrade of the offseason and one the stud count barely noticed.

Then the auction, and the roster went to {{f.team.0008.active_roster_current}}. Prescott replaced Deshaun Watson, Barkley took the lead backfield job, Murray filled the superflex, Parker Washington took a flex. Committed cap went from {{f.team.0008.cap_preauction}} to {{f.team.0008.cap_current_spent}}, leaving {{f.team.0008.cap_current_room}} — enough for one minimum body and a firm handshake. Studs went from {{f.team.0008.studs_opening}} to {{f.team.0008.studs_current}}, holes from {{f.team.0008.holes_opening}} to {{f.team.0008.holes_current}}.

Almost nothing Keith starts today was carried in on an old contract. Goedert, Christian Watson and Henderson are the survivors and none of them is why this team ranks where it does. He built this in one offseason, which is the most impressive thing about it.

Two auctions, two months apart, two completely different Keiths. The Expired Rookie Auction in May cost him {{f.team.0008.era_spend}} across {{f.team.0008.era_lots_won}} players: Chris Rodriguez, Kayshon Boutte, Michael Mayer, Will McDonald, Kendre Miller. Rodriguez was traded before he played a down, Boutte and Mayer both grade replacement-level, and McDonald and Miller were dropped as make-room later in the summer. The entire May haul is either gone or on the bench.

The Free Agent Auction in late July is where the team actually came from: {{f.team.0008.faa_lots_won}} players for {{f.team.0008.faa_spend}}. Prescott alone took {{f.team.0008.top_buy_price}} — {{f.team.0008.top_buy_pct_of_spend}} of the whole budget, and the most contested item he won all summer.

He bought four quarterbacks there. Prescott and Murray start and both grade honestly. Jacoby Brissett, at the cheapest price of the quarterbacks he kept, grades Replacement-level QB and has not moved off the bench. Mac Jones was released in September. Buying a third and fourth quarterback after solving the position is the kind of thing you do at two in the morning when the auction is still open and you are bored.

The bottom of the market is where he is genuinely sharp. Cam Little, Tommy Townsend, Nick Bolton, Josh Hines-Allen and Chamarri Conner all came cheap, which is the correct way to fill the slots ADP refuses to price. Parker Washington is the one bargain with a starting job attached. It is the same instinct as the defense policy — find the thing nobody is bidding on, take it, move on.

Keith made {{f.team.0008.contracts_count}} contract moves. Cam Little, Trey Benson, Brian Robinson, Charlie Kolar, Jack Strand, Jacob Saylors and Stefon Diggs all signed at the league minimum. Diggs at the minimum is the best-priced deal in the set by a distance.

Chig Okonkwo is the one to argue about. He grades Replacement-level TE, he sits behind Goedert, and he was signed above the minimum — but the deal is front-loaded, so most of its total value is paid this season and the back years cost almost nothing. That is a defensible structure for a bet that has not come in yet: it is expensive now precisely so it stops being expensive later. Still a replacement-level tight end on a multi-year deal, though.

The Puka Nacua paperwork is easy to misread. Shawn Blake extended Nacua in May, before the trade. What Real Deal Creel did was cut Nacua's salary mid-auction — freeing {{f.team.0008.restructure_room_freed}} of bidding room at exactly the moment it was worth having — and then put it straight back afterwards, ending on the salary and total value it started with. A maneuver, not a contract.

There were {{f.team.0008.trades_count}} trades and the three-way is the one people will remember, because three-way trades essentially do not happen in this league — this is the only completed one on record, and Keith built it. He sent McMillan, his own first-rounder for next year, Chris Rodriguez and Omar Cooper, and received Nacua. It was not a two-team swap dressed up: C-Town Chivalry separately sent Drake London and {{f.team.0008.trade_blind_bid_cash}} of blind-bid cash to Blake Bombers to make the thing balance. That is what a real price looks like.

He is not short a first-round pick next year despite spending his own, because he had already taken HammerTime's in April for Kenneth Walker. Same asset class, different owner's name on it. The last trade sent George Karlaftis, a startable defender, to the Hawks for a small upgrade in draft slot — which, given how the defense looks in September, reads worse now than it did in August.

Removals ran to {{f.team.0008.roster_removals_total}} bodies, of which only {{f.team.0008.cuts_count}} were contracts carried into the year and released. {{f.team.0008.waiver_swaps}} were the make-room half of a waiver claim and {{f.team.0008.inyear_flyers}} were signed and discarded inside the same offseason — which is exactly what {{f.team.0008.idp_adds_alltime}} career pickups looks like up close. Blake Watson looks like a cut with relief attached and is not: he was on the taxi squad, his salary never touched the cap, and dropping him freed nothing. Penalties charged this season come to {{f.team.0008.cuts_penalty_2026}}, with {{f.team.0008.cuts_penalty_2027_deferred}} deferred to next year.

The rookie class runs to {{f.team.0008.rookie_picks_count}} picks. KC Concepcion came from the best slot of the group and the redraft market has not caught up to him yet. Omar Cooper Jr. was traded before playing a down. De'Zhaun Stribling grades Mid WR3. Sonny Styles and Zion Young are defenders, and neither the redraft board nor the production model can value them — the board does not price the position and the model needs an NFL season that has not happened. That is missing information, not a bad grade.

Real Deal Creel finished {{f.team.0008.composite_rank}} of {{f.league.teams}} and the offense is not the reason. Nacua is Elite WR1, Prescott Mid QB1, Barkley Mid RB1, and the backfield runs three deep. That is a playoff offense assembled in one offseason from a roster that in April was mostly a list of names.

The verdict on the defense depends entirely on whether you believe the plan. He is {{f.team.0008.idp_adds_rank}} in the league in defenders acquired, all-time, by a margin that is frankly ridiculous, and he did it while spending {{f.team.0008.idp_auction_share}} of his auction money on the position. That gets him {{f.team.0008.idp_ppw_rank}} of {{f.league.teams}} in what his defenders actually score. Cheap and fourth is a good deal. It has also never been first, and at some point the question stops being whether the strategy works and becomes whether it wins.

The one thing to fix is smaller and entirely self-inflicted: he sold a startable defender in August for a pick and then opened the season starting three men the waiver wire would replace for free. He will have replaced them by Week Four — he always does. Buy the star, mine the rest. It is a real strategy and it is one good linebacker short of a title.
